$comment: Everyday stories, noun Screen, part 2 of 4 (panelAction, panelDataSource, panelFieldBinding, panelWidget, widget, cellGrid, mapSpec). Same style rules as stories-pilot.json. Owner reviews each part.

stories.cellGrid.colField: A cinema stores each seat as its own row, and the seat plan is drawn from them. Column field names the whole-number box that says in which column a cell sits, counting from zero. Without it NPDev would not know where to draw the seat.
stories.cellGrid.colsField: Some cinema rooms have 12 seats per row, others 20. Columns field names an optional box of the main record that holds the number of columns of this particular board. When it is empty, the default column count is used.
stories.cellGrid.defaultCols: A new cinema room has not said how wide it is. Default columns is the number of columns the board falls back to when no column count is given. Ten is used if you say nothing.
stories.cellGrid.defaultRows: The same new room has not said how many rows it has. Default rows is the number of rows the board falls back to when no row count is given. Ten is used if you say nothing.
stories.cellGrid.layout: A seat plan is a neat square grid, but a board game map looks better as a honeycomb. Layout chooses the shape of the cells: square, which is the default, or hexagonal, where every other row is shifted half a cell and the cells are round.
stories.cellGrid.palette: To paint the seat plan, the staff pick from a small set of things: 'free', 'reserved', 'broken'. Palette says where that set comes from: a query, and which of its boxes give each choice its label, picture and colour.
stories.cellGrid.rowField: Each seat row of the cinema knows its place on the plan. Row field names the whole-number box that says in which row a cell sits, counting from zero.
stories.cellGrid.rowsField: Rooms differ in depth as well as in width. Rows field names an optional box of the main record that holds the number of rows of this board. When it is empty, the default row count is used.
stories.cellGrid.valueField: When staff paint a cell as 'reserved', the cell has to remember it. Value field names the box of the cell that receives the id of the painted choice. If it is a reference, it must point to the same concept the palette comes from.
stories.mapSpec.center: A courier map should open where the courier is, not in the middle of the ocean. Center is the starting view: 'me', which asks the browser for the person's location politely, or a fixed 'latitude,longitude' such as a city centre.
stories.mapSpec.label: A pin on a map of delivery points is more useful with a name beside it. Label names the box, or an expression, that gives each pin its text, such as the customer's name.
stories.mapSpec.lat: To place a pin, the map needs to know how far north or south it is. Lat names the box, or an expression, that holds the latitude of each row.
stories.mapSpec.lng: And it needs to know how far east or west. Lng names the box, or an expression, that holds the longitude of each row.
stories.mapSpec.pickPoints: A taxi app asks where to pick the passenger up and where to drop them off. On a form with a map, pick points are the places the person taps on the map, each one filling in the latitude and longitude boxes you named, such as 'pick-up' and 'drop-off'.
stories.mapSpec.tiles: A map is drawn from small square pictures called tiles, and they come from some provider. Tiles names the setting that holds the address pattern of that provider. If you say nothing, the open OpenStreetMap tiles are used, with their credit line.
stories.panelAction.binding: A back-office button can do several kinds of work: run a query, change a concept's rows, call a procedure or start a flow. Binding picks which of the four this button does.
stories.panelAction.concept: A button that creates a customer must know which kind of record it creates. Concept names it. It is used by the buttons that run a query or a change on a concept.
stories.panelAction.contentType: An 'Export orders' button hands the person a file, and the browser needs to know what kind of file, such as a spreadsheet. Content type is that label, for example text/csv. It is required when the button returns a download.
stories.panelAction.dataSource: A 'Refund' button drawn next to each row has to know which list of rows it belongs to. Data source names it. It is required when the button is drawn once per row.
stories.panelAction.enabledWhen: A 'Ship' button should be clickable only when the order is paid. Enabled when is a condition: the button works only while it is true, and is greyed out otherwise.
stories.panelAction.explainability: Later, an auditor asks why a 'Write off balance' button exists. Explainability is a free note for AI helpers and auditors saying why the action is there. NPDev stores it and does not act on it.
stories.panelAction.filename: When the person downloads the orders export, the file should be called 'orders.csv', not 'download'. Filename is the name offered to the browser. It is required when the button returns a download.
stories.panelAction.flow: A 'Reopen ticket' button has several steps to run. Flow names the flow, the recipe of steps, that the button starts. It is used by the buttons whose binding is flow.
stories.panelAction.inputFields: Before 'Refund' can run, the clerk has to type the amount and the reason. Input fields lists the boxes NPDev asks the person to fill in first. What they type is handed to the flow as its input.
stories.panelAction.label: 'Approve refund' is clearer than 'Action 2'. Label is the caption written on the button. It can be plain text or one text per language.
stories.panelAction.metadata: Whoever added a button wants to keep a note beside it, such as 'asked for by finance'. Metadata is a free notebook on the action. NPDev carries it along unchanged and does nothing with it.
stories.panelAction.name: Two buttons in the same panel must not be mixed up. Name is the button's own name, and it must be unique inside the panel.
stories.panelAction.operation: A button tied to a concept can read, add, change or remove rows. Operation chooses which: query, create, update or delete. It is used by the buttons whose binding is a concept query or a concept change.
stories.panelAction.permissionRequirements: Only the finance team should even see 'Write off balance'. Permission requirements lists the permissions a person must hold to see and run the button. Anyone without them does not see it.
stories.panelAction.procedure: A 'Recalculate prices' button has its logic written once, as a flow. Procedure names that flow, and the button runs it. It is used by the buttons whose binding is procedure.
stories.panelAction.resultAs: An 'Export orders' button should hand over a real file, not a page of data on the screen. Result as, set to download, makes the flow's answer arrive as a file the browser saves. It only works on buttons whose binding is procedure and needs a filename and a content type.
stories.panelAction.scope: 'Refresh all' belongs to the whole panel, but 'Refund' belongs to one row. Scope says which: panel draws the button once with no row, and row draws it on every row of a list and starts it with that row's id.
stories.panelAction.visibleWhen: A 'Cancel order' button is useless on an order that has already shipped. Visible when is a condition: the button is shown only while it is true.
stories.panelDataSource.addFormFields: When someone adds a new line to the table, the form should ask for item and quantity, and nothing else. Add form fields lists the boxes of that small form.
stories.panelDataSource.childField: Order lines know which order they belong to. Child field names the box of the lines that holds the link to the order, the parent.
stories.panelDataSource.concept: A panel of customers has to read customers from somewhere. Concept names the kind of record this data source reads rows of.
stories.panelDataSource.name: A panel can have several lists of rows, for instance 'orders' and 'order lines'. Name is the data source's own name, and bindings, widgets and row buttons refer to it by that name.
stories.panelDataSource.onRowLoad: The list of customers comes from the database, but the screen also wants a 'days since last purchase' column that is worked out by a flow. On row load names that flow. It adds details to the rows that already exist and never adds, drops or reorders them, or it fails loudly.
stories.panelDataSource.params: A query 'orders of a city' needs to know which city. Params hands it the answer: for each parameter, a fixed value or an expression. Flows get their answers the same way.
stories.panelDataSource.parentDataSource: Under the table of orders, the table of that order's lines appears. Parent data source names the list this one hangs under, the order list, which makes a master-detail pair.
stories.panelDataSource.parentField: To find the lines of an order, NPDev has to know which box of the order ties to them. Parent field names the box of the parent row that links to the child rows.
stories.panelDataSource.procedure: Sometimes the rows are not stored anywhere, but worked out by a flow: a ranking, a forecast. Procedure replaces the normal row source entirely with that flow's output.
stories.panelDataSource.query: A panel of late deliveries should read the rows that a query called 'late deliveries' already returns. Query names it, so the panel shows exactly those rows.
stories.panelDataSource.rowOps: In the order lines table the clerk may add and remove lines, but in a table of payments they may only add. Row ops lists what a person may do with the rows of this nested list: add, delete or both.
stories.panelDataSource.totalField: Under a table of order lines, a footer shows how many items there are in all. Total field names the numeric box to add up, and the sum of every row currently displayed is shown at the bottom. It is only a display total, worked out in the browser.
stories.panelFieldBinding.editable: In the order panel, the clerk may change the quantity but not the price. Editable says that the person may edit this box in the panel.
stories.panelFieldBinding.enabledWhen: The 'discount reason' box should be editable only once a discount has been given. Enabled when is a condition: the box can be edited only while it is true.
stories.panelFieldBinding.field: Each line of a panel has to say which box of the data it is about. Field names the box being bound.
stories.panelFieldBinding.readonlyWhen: Once an invoice is posted, its amount should no longer change. Read-only when is a condition: while it is true, the box can be seen but not edited.
stories.panelFieldBinding.source: A panel can read from several lists, and the 'customer name' box has to say which one it comes from. Source names the data source. If you say nothing, the panel's main one is used.
stories.panelFieldBinding.ui: The 'price' box in a panel should look like money, with a currency, and 'notes' should be a big text area. UI carries those presentation hints for this one binding.
stories.panelFieldBinding.visibleWhen: A 'cancellation reason' box is noise on an order that has not been cancelled. Visible when is a condition: the box is shown only while it is true.
stories.panelWidget.aggregate: A tile on a wall-board says how many orders there are, or how much they add up to. Aggregate chooses the calculation: count, sum, average, minimum or maximum. Count is the default, and the others need a field to work on.
stories.panelWidget.chart: Sales per region can be drawn as bars, as a line or as a doughnut. Chart picks one of the three. It is for chart widgets only.
stories.panelWidget.dataSource: A tile has to count something, and a chart has to draw something. Data source names the list of the panel the widget reads from. It is required for tiles, charts and tables.
stories.panelWidget.field: A tile showing 'total sold' has to know which box to add up. Field names the numeric box that sum, average, minimum and maximum work on.
stories.panelWidget.filter: A tile 'open orders' should count only the orders whose status is 'OPEN'. Filter names a box and the text it must equal, and only those rows are counted.
stories.panelWidget.groupBy: To draw 'orders per city', the chart needs to know what makes the groups. Group by names the box whose different values become the bars or slices. It is for charts only.
stories.panelWidget.kind: A wall-board mixes a big number, a chart, a bar of buttons, a history of what was done this session and a table of rows. Kind picks which one this widget is: tile, chart, actions, history or table. The action bar and the history may appear once each.
stories.panelWidget.span: The chart of the week needs more room than a small tile. Span is the width of a widget in a grid of four columns, from one to four. One is the default.
stories.panelWidget.title: A number alone means little, so a tile says 'Orders waiting' above it. Title is the heading of the widget.
stories.widget.chart: A dashboard shows sales per region. Chart picks how the bars are drawn: as bars, as a line or as a doughnut. It is for chart widgets.
stories.widget.groupBy: A chart over a screen's rows can count 'tickets per status'. Group by names the box of that screen's concept, and every different value becomes one point, with the rows counted.
stories.widget.kind: A dashboard screen mixes a big number, a chart, a table, a map and a short list. Kind picks which one a widget is: tile, chart, table, map or list.
stories.widget.screen: A dashboard can show the table of late orders without rebuilding it. Screen names an existing screen to embed, and it works for tables, lists and maps.
stories.widget.span: A map needs more room than a tile on the same dashboard. Span is the width of a widget in a grid of four columns, from one to four.
stories.widget.title: A dashboard tile says 'Active rides' above its number. Title is the heading of the widget.
stories.widget.value: A tile saying 'requested rides' is worked out by a short expression, such as counting the rides whose status is requested. Value holds that expression. A chart holds one expression per label, one point each.
